Q: How to configure RestClient timeout in Spring Boot 4? A:

Finally found an example in the Spring Boot IO docs that shows how to use ClientHttpRequestFactory to apply the settings explicitly:

If you need to apply other customization in addition to an SSL bundle, you can use the HttpClientSettings class with ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder:

[...] 
HttpClientSettings settings = HttpClientSettings
    .ofSslBundle(sslBundles.getBundle("mybundle"))
    .withReadTimeout(Duration.ofMinutes(2));
ClientHttpRequestFactory requestFactory = ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder
    .detect()
    .build(settings);
this.restClient = restClientBuilder
    .baseUrl("https://example.org")
    .requestFactory(requestFactory)
    .build();
[...]

(my formatting and only showing relevant lines of code)

However, based on these Spring Boot IO docs, I believe our HttpClientConfig approach proposed in the Question, although correct, is unnecessarily complex for our simple use case.

Because we only need a default RestClient with some custom HTTP client timeouts, we decided to use global configuration instead:

# application.yml
spring:
  http:
    clients:
      connect-timeout: 5s
      read-timeout: 5s
...

In addition, wherever a RestClient is used in our code base, we now inject the Spring-Boot-managed RestClient.Builder, instead of the RestClient bean from the HttpClientConfig class, following the Spring Boot IO docs:

To make the scope of any customizations as narrow as possible, inject the auto-configured RestClient.Builder and then call its methods as required. RestClient.Builder instances are stateful: Any change on the builder is reflected in all clients subsequently created with it. [...]

As a result we can remove the HttpClientConfig class altogether.

Q: Is injecting MainPage into App and registering it as Singleton a recommended approach in .NET MAUI? A:

I can give you some information about your questions 2 and 3. The reality is that even the guys who drive this platform may turn out to be clueless about it.

If you read docs, you may come across this:

For most .NET MAUI use cases:

  • Use AddTransient<T> for pages and view models to get a fresh instance on each navigation.

  • Use AddSingleton<T> for shared services such as database connections, settings, or caches.

Which is pretty much what we knew all along. It is logical. Pretty much non-optional for MAUI's original - Xamarin. Original shell needed to be able to re-create new page when needed, and managed the life cycle internally.

You do not follow this rule - runtime exception. This is what I do ever since MAUI came along. Apps in Appstore/Google play, everything works fine. I am using Shell navigation, however.

The interesting situation is that despite the docs stating "transient for pages", "singleton for services", taking a look at what examples the MAUI team provides to you - you will notice that they do EXACTLY THE OPPOSITE.

One page above you see Transient Service, followed by Singleton Main. Then one page bellow you see how they make extension methods to register both the View Models and the Views as singletons, and the services as transient.

At some point (honestly no idea when), the situation for double-registering routes and changing from transient to singleton changed. It doesn't seem to be causing crashes. And you will most likely not encounter any lifetime related issues, no matter what you do.

Your best bet is good end-to-end tests, now and every time you upgrade your MAUI workload and community toolkit. This is the current best practice.
